title: FDA uses AI to choose where to concentrate food inspections; an imported-seafood pilot ran for years
summary: FDA reports that its seafood-import model recommended samples and that Elsa helped identify inspection targets. Neither report quantifies added hazards detected or illnesses prevented.
account: Civil Eats reported on 27 May 2025 that FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, appearing before a Senate committee the previous week, said the agency was using AI to identify where to concentrate food inspections and that AI can sometimes find patterns faster than people, adding that a human reviews the information. The article notes that FDA had been working for several years on a pilot focused on imported seafood and had announced an agency-wide generative AI rollout, with an FDA spokesperson saying all centers would run on a unified platform by 30 June; a 2 June update records the launch of FDA's generative tool Elsa, said to be used in part to identify high-priority inspection targets. Jaydee Hanson of the Center for Food Safety is quoted on the risks of using AI amid staff cuts. No inspection outcome, detection or recall attributable to the AI is given. FDA’s August 22, 2022 update states that its operational seafood model returned sampling recommendations to reviewers at all 328 U.S. ports during February–July 2021. Its June 2, 2025 Elsa announcement describes a separate LLM tool in GovCloud that helped identify inspection targets. These original reports give no numerical improvement in detection or health outcomes.
purpose: Prioritize food inspection targets, including imported seafood, using pattern recognition over agency data.
system: FDA AI inspection-targeting tools (imported seafood pilot; Elsa generative AI)
developer: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (details not in the cited source)
taxonomy_note: Statements of use only; the type names better-targeted inspections, not a documented outcome.

ratings.reason: No figure on inspections targeted, violations found or seafood shipments flagged appears in the source.
No contamination detection or recall is attributed to the AI.

ai_role.statement: FDA’s original reports describe a seafood-import model that returned sampling recommendations to reviewers and Elsa’s separate use in identifying inspection priorities. The seafood pilot operated at all 328 U.S. ports from February through July 2021; Elsa launched on June 2, 2025 in a secure GovCloud environment. These sources establish the tools’ reported use, but do not quantify improved detection or health outcomes.

fields.account: Civil Eats reported on 27 May 2025 that FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, appearing before a Senate committee the previous week, said the agency was using AI to identify where to concentrate food inspections and that AI can sometimes find patterns faster than people, adding that a human reviews the information. The article notes that FDA had been working for several years on a pilot focused on imported seafood and had announced an agency-wide generative AI rollout, with an FDA spokesperson saying all centers would run on a unified platform by 30 June; a 2 June update records the launch of FDA's generative tool Elsa, said to be used in part to identify high-priority inspection targets. Jaydee Hanson of the Center for Food Safety is quoted on the risks of using AI amid staff cuts. No inspection outcome, detection or recall attributable to the AI is given. FDA’s August 22, 2022 update states that its operational seafood model returned sampling recommendations to reviewers at all 328 U.S. ports during February–July 2021. Its June 2, 2025 Elsa announcement describes a separate LLM tool in GovCloud that helped identify inspection targets. These original reports give no numerical improvement in detection or health outcomes.
